subtype: Approach: picks a quick rough sketch when the problem is new and the time is short [Thinking]
passage:
Chaitanya here. Last October the fest coordinator, Karthik, found me in the corridor at lunch and said the banner artist had dropped out, and could I have a design by five.
Normally I would open a big sheet and plan colours for an hour. That day I thought: I have a few hours and I've never done this size before, so a neat plan would eat the whole afternoon. So I took a scrap page and sketched three rough layouts, ten minutes in all. The name in the middle. The name on a slant. The name over a big sun.
I showed all three to Karthik, who tapped the slanted one. I spent the rest of the time drawing that layout properly, and it went up on the gate at five.

qa.q: How many layouts did Chaitanya sketch?
qa.a: Chaitanya sketched three rough layouts, ten minutes in all.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya think about making a neat plan for the banner?
qa.a: Chaitanya thought a neat plan would eat the whole afternoon, so decided quick sketches suited a new size and short time.

qa.q: What could Chaitanya do if there had been a whole week for the banner?
qa.a: Chaitanya could plan colours and lettering more carefully, since a longer time makes a polished plan worth the effort.

qa.q: How might Karthik see the three sketches?
qa.a: Karthik needed a design by five and could choose at once by tapping the slanted one, so probably found it helpful to see options quickly.

grounding: A teenager asked at short notice to design a fest banner makes a few rough sketches and picks one instead of a polished plan.

subtype: Approach: acts quickly when time is short and the situation is urgent [Thinking]
passage:
The hostel talent night was loud and warm. Someone was singing on stage when Farida saw Harsha, standing at the back, sway and fold to the floor. There was no time for anything clever.
"Harsha's fainted!" Farida shouted, and the music stopped. "Get the warden, now! Someone call the hostel nurse!" Two students ran. Farida knelt beside Harsha, asked the others to step back, and stayed there talking softly until the warden arrived, took charge and called for a doctor.
A minute later Harsha's eyes opened, confused. Farida's hands were still shaking. "You're okay, we're here," Farida said. The warden thanked Farida for not waiting.

qa.q: What did Farida shout when Harsha fainted?
qa.a: Farida shouted that Harsha had fainted and asked for the warden and the hostel nurse.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling right after Harsha opened their eyes?
qa.a: Farida was shaken and relieved, shown by the trembling hands and the soft words.

qa.q: Why was acting at once the right approach here?
qa.a: There was no time for a detailed plan, so calling for help and staying beside Harsha was the wise choice while the warden and a doctor took over.

qa.q: How might Harsha have felt on waking up?
qa.a: Harsha probably felt confused and a little scared, and may have been comforted to hear Farida say they were there.

grounding: A student sees a friend faint at a hostel event and acts at once, calling for help, since there is no time for a detailed plan.

subtype: Approach: takes time and sleeps on it when the decision is slow and important [Thinking]
passage:
Beta, sit down. It's Mridul Mama. You asked how I decided about studying further? I was twenty-one, with a job offer in one hand and a place for a master's in the other, and both letters said to reply within the season. Nobody was standing over me with a clock.
So I gave myself a month. First I wrote down facts: fees, how long, where each path led. Then I sat with my parents after dinner, three evenings, listening more than talking. My sister Lalremsiami phoned from Aizawl and said, "You keep saying you should, but never that you want to."
That sentence sat in my chest for a week. I slept on it, and one morning I knew. I took the master's.

qa.q: How long did the decision take Mridul?
qa.a: Mridul gave the decision a month.

qa.q: What did Mridul feel after Lalremsiami's sentence?
qa.a: The sentence sat in Mridul's chest for a week, so it stirred something and made Mridul think about wanting, not only about what should be done.

qa.q: Which step in the story helped Mridul most, and why?
qa.a: Talking with Lalremsiami helped most, because the words showed the difference between what Mridul should do and what Mridul wanted, and no deadline forced speed.

qa.q: How does Lalremsiami see Mridul's choice?
qa.a: Lalremsiami noticed that Mridul kept saying should, never want, so may have felt concerned and wanted an honest look at the wish.

grounding: Weighing further study, a student lets the decision take a month, gathering facts and talking to family, since no deadline forces speed.

subtype: Approach: plans alone for a personal decision [Thinking]
passage:
I'm Farhan, Omkar's roommate. Last Sunday I watched Omkar plan a study timetable for the new term. People offered ideas: our floor mate said to copy his, and a senior said to ask the toppers. Omkar said thanks and shut the door.
Then he sat at the desk with a blank page and wrote quickly: mornings after tea for the hard subjects, a walk after lunch, light reading at night. "I know when my head works," he told me when I asked. "Nobody else does."
He finished in twenty minutes and pinned it up. I can't say whether he was sure or just tired of advice, but he didn't change a line all week.

qa.q: How long did Omkar take to finish the timetable?
qa.a: Omkar finished in twenty minutes.

qa.q: What does Omkar seem to feel about other people's advice?
qa.a: Omkar seems confident in his own knowledge, saying nobody else knows when his head works, though Farhan cannot be sure he was not simply tired of advice.

qa.q: What could Omkar do if the timetable stopped working?
qa.a: Omkar could adjust it after a week by noticing which slots he actually used, since he knows his own habits best.

qa.q: How does Farhan see Omkar's way of planning?
qa.a: Farhan watched and admits he cannot tell whether Omkar was sure or tired of advice, but saw that the timetable stayed unchanged all week.

grounding: A student choosing his own study schedule thinks it through alone since he knows his own habits.

subtype: Approach: plans as a group when several people share the result [Thinking]
passage:
So, the floor rules. I'm Sonali, the floor rep on the third floor. There were twelve of us and everyone was bothered about something: late music, the shared kettle, guests.
I could have written a list and stuck it on the door, but it would have been ignored by the next day. So I called a meeting on Sunday, brought biscuits and said, we all live here, so let's decide together. Irfan, from the end room, said late music was the worst thing. Others argued about the kettle. It took two hours.
In the end we agreed on quiet after eleven, a kettle rota and guests signed in. Nobody loved every rule, but nobody could say it was forced on them. Two months later, the sheet is still up, and people actually follow it.

qa.q: How many people lived on Sonali's floor?
qa.a: There were twelve of them.

qa.q: Why did Sonali choose a meeting over writing a list?
qa.a: Sonali knew a list would be ignored by the next day and wanted the floor to feel it was their own decision.

qa.q: What could the floor do if the rules started to slip?
qa.a: They could hold another short meeting and change the rota together, since rules made together are easier to keep than ones from one person.

qa.q: How did Irfan see the problems on the floor?
qa.a: Irfan from the end room said late music was the worst thing, so probably wanted the meeting to deal with noise most of all.

grounding: A hostel floor deciding on shared rules holds a meeting, since a plan made by one person would not be followed by the rest.

subtype: Approach: uses one method for every problem out of habit [Pitfall]
passage:
Monday. Sangeeta has to make a poster for the arts fest. She opens the colour-coded timetable app she uses for exams: sketch 9 to 10, colours 10 to 12, lettering 2 to 3. She sits down at nine with a pencil, and nothing comes.
Wednesday. The same block has moved forward twice. "Idea generation, ten minutes," the app says. She stares at a blank page. Nandini asks, "Want to just doodle for a bit?" "It's not in the schedule."
Friday. The sheet is still empty and every block on the timetable is red. Sangeeta rubs her eyes and opens the app again to move the blocks once more.

qa.q: What does Sangeeta have to make for the arts fest?
qa.a: Sangeeta has to make a poster.

qa.q: What does Sangeeta feel when saying that doodling is not in the schedule?
qa.a: Sangeeta feels tense and stuck, holding tightly to the timetable even though it has not helped.

qa.q: What different approach might suit the poster better?
qa.a: Sangeeta could start with loose doodles for a short time, since creative work often starts better without fixed blocks.

qa.q: How might Nandini feel watching the timetable move again?
qa.a: Nandini offered to doodle, so may feel concerned and a bit helpless watching Sangeeta turn down a loose start.

grounding: A student who likes detailed timetables uses one for creative work, where a loose start would suit better, and feels blocked.

subtype: Approach: uses working backward when there is a fixed date [Thinking]
passage:
Sunday. The thesis is due on 12 December, with no extension. Tonight I stopped worrying and counted back from that date. Proofreading and formatting: week of 8 December. All references done: week of 1 December. Chapter four finished: 24 November. Chapter three: 17 November.
So this week I only need the first draft of chapter three, and it's a third done already. It's odd how small this week looks next to the whole thing. If I counted forward I'd always think there was more time. The date fixes the end, and the end fixes each week.
I've pinned the list above my desk.
Pallavi

qa.q: When is the thesis due?
qa.a: The thesis is due on 12 December.

qa.q: What does Pallavi feel about this week's target?
qa.a: Pallavi feels calmer and a little surprised, because this week looks small next to the whole thesis.

qa.q: What else could Pallavi add to make the plan safer?
qa.a: Pallavi could leave a spare week before the date, since delays such as illness or a slow chapter are possible.

qa.q: How might a supervisor see the weekly list?
qa.a: A supervisor would see a clear plan with dates, and could check each week whether chapter three and chapter four are finished on time.

grounding: A student with a fixed submission date counts back from it to set weekly targets, since the deadline defines the goal.

subtype: Approach: matches effort to reversibility, deciding fast on reversible choices and slow on one-way ones [Thinking]
passage:
Naveen's phone plan ended on the first, and the shop near the metro station offered five options. He read two, picked the middle one in five minutes and paid.
"Wasn't there a cheaper one?" asked Rukmini, a friend, over tea.
"Probably. I can switch next month if I hate it," he said.
The rental contract for the new flat was a different matter. For three weeks he read every clause twice, asked the owner about notice periods and compared two other flats in the same lane. He wrote questions on his phone and crossed them off one by one.
"Why so slow this time?" Rukmini asked.
"Because if I sign the wrong one, I'm stuck for a year."

qa.q: How long did Naveen take to choose the phone plan?
qa.a: Naveen picked the plan in five minutes.

qa.q: What did Naveen feel about the phone plan and the contract, and why?
qa.a: Naveen felt relaxed about the plan because it can be switched next month, and careful about the contract because signing the wrong one means being stuck for a year.

qa.q: What could Naveen do to make the rental decision more secure?
qa.a: Naveen could ask a knowledgeable person to read the contract, since a one-way choice deserves extra checking.

qa.q: How might Rukmini see the difference in speed?
qa.a: Rukmini asked why the contract was so slow, so at first found it puzzling, but Naveen's answer explains it.

grounding: A student picks a phone plan quickly because it can be changed, but takes weeks over a rental contract that is hard to leave.

subtype: Approach: uses brainstorming for a novel problem with no known answer [Thinking]
passage:
Sudha's hardware shop in the market town had a new problem. Farmers could not leave their fields at harvest, and kept asking for pipes and hinges to be brought out to them. Nobody knew how to do it.
On Saturday evening after closing, Sudha, Farida and the two helpers sat on the shop floor with a roll of paper. "Say any idea, even silly ones," said Sudha. A boy on a cycle. A phone list of orders. A weekly round to the farms with the pickup. Someone joked about a drone.
The paper filled up and nobody said no. When the tea was cold they had eighteen ideas, and they circled three that would cost little to try. "Nobody here has done this before," said Farida, "so we'll have to invent it."

qa.q: How many ideas did the team have at the end?
qa.a: They had eighteen ideas.

qa.q: What did Sudha want from the team by saying even silly ideas were welcome?
qa.a: Sudha wanted everyone to feel free and hopeful about sharing, because there was no known answer to copy.

qa.q: What could the team do after circling three ideas?
qa.a: They could try the cheapest idea on a small scale and see how farmers react, since only real use shows what works.

qa.q: How might the farmers see the new plan?
qa.a: Farmers who cannot leave their fields at harvest may welcome pipes and hinges being brought out to them.

grounding: A team facing a new customer problem gathers many ideas before choosing, since there is no precedent to copy.

subtype: Approach: uses precedent for a familiar problem [Thinking]
passage:
Parul: Starting the January workshop plan today.
Shankar: From scratch?
Parul: No. Last year's schedule. Same three sessions, same lunch break, same feedback form.
Shankar: Won't it feel stale?
Parul: It ran smoothly with sixty people and the comments were good. I'm only changing the dates and the venue, since the hall isn't free.
Shankar: Fair. I'll check the new hall's projector 🙂
Parul: Perfect. The old registration form goes out tomorrow with the new dates.
Shankar: Do we need a meeting?
Parul: Ten minutes on Thursday, that's all.
Shankar: Faster than I expected.
Parul: It's been solved once already 👍

qa.q: How many people came to last year's workshop?
qa.a: Sixty people came to it.

qa.q: What does Parul feel about reusing last year's plan?
qa.a: Parul feels confident about it, because it ran smoothly and the comments were good.

qa.q: What could Parul do to keep the reused plan from going stale?
qa.a: Parul could read last year's feedback forms and change one small thing they mention, since a familiar plan can still improve.

qa.q: How does Shankar see the shortcut at first?
qa.a: Shankar first wonders if it will feel stale, then accepts it as fair and is surprised by how fast it goes.

grounding: An experienced coordinator plans a routine workshop by reusing last year's schedule, changing only dates and venue.
